h1: How to monitor competitor prices automatically
answer: List the exact competitor pages and the price on each you care about, then have a tool open them once a day, compare each price with the one it saw last time, and tell you only when one changes.
Treat a page that would not load or a price it could not find as its own alert, because a broken check that reads as "no change" is how price monitoring quietly fails.

body.p: Price trackers win on catalogues: matching thousands of products across shops is their job. For a dozen software pricing pages or local competitors’ menus, a browser agent or a weekly check is simpler.

sections.h2: Stay on the right side of the sites you read

body.p: Reading a public pricing page once a day is what any customer does. Keep it that way: stay on public pages, check no more than you need, and stop at bot checks. A site’s robots.txt file says which parts it wants automated visitors to avoid; Google notes that it cannot enforce anything and that well-behaved crawlers follow it.

On the law, a US appeals court said in hiQ v. LinkedIn that scraping public data was likely not "without authorization" under the federal anti-hacking law, while drawing a line at data behind a login. Site terms and contract claims still apply, and laws differ by country. If a page needs a login or shows a CAPTCHA, take that as a no.

method.h2: How to set it up, step by step

steps.title: Make the list of pages and prices
steps.body: One row per price: competitor, page, plan, the price today. That first price is your baseline.

steps.title: Pick a time of day and keep it
steps.body: Same time each day, so a change shows on the day it happened.

steps.title: Store the last price seen
steps.body: Each check compares with the last one and then replaces it. Without this, you get the same alert every day.

steps.title: Alert only on change, with both numbers
steps.body: "Acme Team plan: $29 to $35" is useful; "prices checked" is not.

steps.title: Alert on failures separately
steps.body: Page did not load, price not found, layout changed: each should say so. A silent failure looks exactly like "no change".

steps.title: Review the list monthly
steps.body: Competitors rename plans and move pages. Update the list when they do.

example.h2: A worked example: a browser agent in 50agents
body: In 50agents this is a browser agent: it uses websites the way a person would, with no app to connect. Tell Captain which pages to watch; each morning it opens them in its own browser, reads the prices, and tells you what changed. It uses the lightest source first, opens at most 15 pages a run, and never tries to get past a CAPTCHA or bot check: it gets the price another way or tells you it could not.

wrong.title: A broken check reads as "no change"
wrong.body: The page moved and the tool found no price, so nothing changed. Make "price not found" an alert of its own.

wrong.title: The same alert every day
wrong.body: The last price was never updated after the first alert. Store the new price each time.

wrong.title: Noise from promotions
wrong.body: A weekend sale triggers two alerts. Say whether you care about sale prices, and note them as such.

wrong.title: Blocked or challenged
wrong.body: You checked too often or the site does not want bots. Check less, and if a page shows a bot check, stop and drop it from the list.

wrong.title: Monthly and yearly mixed up
wrong.body: The page defaulted to yearly prices one day. Name the billing period in the list and in the alert.

faqs.q: Is it legal to monitor competitor prices?
faqs.a: Reading public pricing pages is common and, in the US, was treated as likely lawful in hiQ v. LinkedIn. Respect site terms, avoid anything behind a login or a CAPTCHA, and check the law where you operate.

faqs.q: How often should I check competitor prices?
faqs.a: Daily is enough for most businesses; retail catalogues with frequent repricing may need more, which is what dedicated price trackers are built for.

faqs.q: Is there a free way to do it?
faqs.a: For a few pages, a weekly check by hand. Pricefy’s free plan covers up to 50 SKUs and 5 competitors with one update a day.
